claims.text: Introducing stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations into refractory high-entropy alloys enhances strength and ductility.
Introducing SCCPs maintains thermal stability.
Introducing SCCPs maintains irradiation stability.
The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy has a nanocrystalline microstructure with reasonable thermal stability and irradiation resistance but limited strength and ductility.
Controlled additions of nanoprecipitate-forming elements followed by tailored heat treatment can induce coherent nanoprecipitates in the alloy matrix.
The coherent nanoprecipitates form stepwise during processing.
The coherent nanoprecipitates are uniformly distributed within the matrix.
The nanoprecipitates impede dislocation movement.
The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate dislocation transmission.
The coherent interfaces relieve stress concentrations that could cause premature crack initiation.
The combination of precipitate strengthening, facilitated dislocation transmission, and stress relief improves both strength and ductility.
SCCPs mitigate irradiation-induced defect buildup.
Relative to an alloy without engineered SCCPs, the SCCP alloy will have higher yield strength at ambient and elevated temperatures.
Relative to an alloy without engineered SCCPs, the SCCP alloy will have improved tensile ductility at ambient temperature.
Relative to an alloy without engineered SCCPs, the SCCP alloy will have improved tensile ductility at elevated temperatures.
The SCCP alloy will retain resistance to grain growth during high-temperature exposure.
The SCCP alloy will retain resistance to irradiation-induced defect accumulation under heavy-ion irradiation and helium implantation.
The benefits should persist up to approximately 800 °C if the nanoprecipitates remain coherent and stable.
The benefits should persist under irradiation provided the nanoprecipitates remain coherent and stable at the applied flux.
Deviations in precipitate size, distribution, or coherence may negate the improvements or cause phase instability.
